rationale: A wins because it knows exactly where the facts stop. Its best line is the discipline in “Do not assert the program is unprofitable or a halo — the only fact is the non-disclosure,” while B lets a punchier but shakier frame carry too much weight: “Patagonia expands a program built to sell you less clothing.” B has useful instincts, especially the service angle, but it keeps turning absence and hypothesis into story premise. That is how a decent pitch becomes a reporter’s follow-up question with teeth.
gaps_in_A: “500,000 resold items is the lead” is only half a lead without timeframe, run rate, or denominator. A names the hole, but the angle still leans on a cumulative number that may be old-news-shaped.

“The retailer that won't say how much money its sustainability story makes” slightly overstates the fact. The update says Patagonia will not disclose resale share of revenue, not the economics of its whole sustainability story.
“Next step: newsjack-detector” is useful but a touch fussy. The all-store repair rollout is already a valid peg; hunting for an outside hook before any drafting could slow a same-day launch pitch.
A misses a clean service-journalism angle around drop-off, mail-in, free basic repairs, and at-cost complex repairs. That is not the sexiest story, but it is a real reader-useful piece.
gaps_in_B: “Patagonia expands a program built to sell you less clothing” is a strong headline and a weak fact. The update does not say Patagonia built Worn Wear to reduce new apparel sales.

“no new apparel line announced alongside this launch” is treated as evidence of restraint. That is reading strategy into silence; B later admits this in the uncomfortable questions, but the angle already spent the check.

“whether a national chain putting free repair drop-off in 70+ stores plus mail-in is evidence the category itself has matured” overreaches without outside market proof. That is a trend hypothesis, not a grounded angle yet.

“How to get Patagonia gear repaired for free now that it's in every store” overpromises. Only basic repairs are free; complex repairs are charged at cost, so the headline is one angry reader away from becoming sloppy.
